heading_path.h2: 1.2 Place value
heading_path.h3: Worked example 1.2: Finding place value in decimal numbers

placement.rationale: This worked example identifies the place values of non-zero digits in a decimal number.

records.evidence_quote: Write down the place values of all the non-zero digits in the following number: 73,025.048
records.prompt_text: Write down the place values of all the non-zero digits in the following number: 73,025.048
records.answer_text:
Step 1: Write the number in a place value table. Show the decimal point clearly in your table.

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
 \hline
 \text{tth} & \text{th} & \text{h} & \text{t} & \text{u} & \text{.} & \text{t} & \text{h} & \text{th} & \text{tth} \\
 (10,000) & (1,000) & (100) & (10) & (1) & \text{.} & (0.1) & (0.01) & (0.001) & (0.0001) \\
 \hline
 7 & 3 & 0 & 2 & 5 & . & 0 & 4 & 8 \\
 \hline
 \end{array}
$$

Step 2: Multiply each non-zero digit by the value of the column it is in.

$7\times10,000=70,000$\
$3\times1,000=3,000$\
$2\times10=20$\
$5\times1=5$\
$4\times 0.01=0.04$\
$8\times 0.001=0.008$

heading_path.h2: 1.4 How to add in groups of ten using place value

placement.rationale: This exposition explains adding groups of ten using place value and shows how values move to the next column.

records.evidence_quote: In the base ten number system, we can have a maximum of 9 digits for one place value. For example, the number 90 means 9 groups of 10, so we have a 9 in the tens place value. We may write it as 9 x 10 = 90. If we add another group of 10, we have 10 x 10 = 100. This means we have 1 group of 100, so we have a 1 in the hu
records.content_text:
In the base ten number system, we can have a maximum of 9 digits for one place value. For example, the number 90 means 9 groups of 10, so we have a 9 in the tens place value. We may write it as 9 x 10 = 90. If we add another group of 10, we have 10 x 10 = 100. This means we have 1 group of 100, so we have a 1 in the hundreds place value. Ten groups of 10 is named one hundred.

Similarly, the number 900 means 9 groups of 100. We may write it as 9 x 100 = 900. So there is a 9 in the hundreds place value. If we add another group of 100, we have 10 x 100 = 1,000. So we will then have a 1 in the thousands place value. Ten groups of 100 is named one thousand.

Here are the names of some large numbers made up of groups of 10.

$$
\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|}
  \hline
    \textbf{Groups} & \textbf{Meaning} & \textbf{Value} &\textbf{Name}  \\
    \hline
     \text{Ten groups of 1,000} & 10\times1,000 & 10,000 & \text{Ten thousand}    \\
    \hline
    \text{Ten groups of 10,000} & 10\times10,000 & 100,000 & \text{One hundred thousand}    \\
    \hline
    \text{Ten groups of 100,000} & 10\times100,000 & 1,000,000 & \text{One million}    \\
    \hline
    \text{Ten groups of 1,000,000} & 10\times1,000,000 & 10,000,000 & \text{Ten million}    \\
    \hline
    \text{Ten groups of 10,000,000} & 10\times10,000,000 & 100,000,000 & \text{One hundred million}    \\
    \hline
    \text{Ten groups of 100,000,000} & 10\times100,000,000 & 1,000,000,000 & \text{One billion}    \\
    \hline
    \text{Ten groups of 1,000,000,000} & 10\times1,000,000,000 & 10,000,000,000 & \text{Ten billion}    \\
    \hline
    \text{Ten groups of 10,000,000,000} & 10\times10,000,000,000 & 100,000,000,000 & \text{One hundred billion}    \\
    \hline
    \text{Ten groups of 100,000,000,000} & 10\times100,000,000,000 & 1,000,000,000,000 & \text{One trillion}    \\
    \hline
     \end{array}
$$

heading_path.h2: 1.4 How to add in groups of ten using place value
heading_path.h3: Beyond the digit 9

placement.rationale: This exposition states the regrouping rule when a place-value digit reaches 9 and one more group is added.

records.evidence_quote: Whenever we reach the digit 9 in any column of a place value table, and then want to add one more group: - the digit 9 becomes 0 - the digit in the column to the left must increase by 1.
records.content_text:
Whenever we reach the digit 9 in any column of a place value table, and then want to add one more group:

- the digit 9 becomes 0
- the digit in the column to the left must increase by 1.

heading_path.h2: 1.4 How to add in groups of ten using place value
heading_path.h3: Worked example 1.3: Dealing with the digit 9

placement.rationale: This worked example adds 10,000 to a whole number using place value regrouping.

records.evidence_quote: Add 10,000 to the number 591,432.
records.prompt_text: Add 10,000 to the number 591,432.
records.answer_text:
Step 1: Write the given number in a place value table. Find the column in which the digit will have to change.

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
 \hline
 \text{hth} & \text{tth} & \text{th} & \text{h} & \text{  t  } & \text{  u  }  \\
  (100,000) & (10,000) & (1,000) & (100) & (10) & (1) \\
 \hline
   5 & 9 & 1 & 4 & 3 & 2  \\
 \hline
 \end{array}
$$

If 10,000 is added, the digit in the column labelled "**tth**" will change.

Step 2: Change the 9 to 0. In the column to the left, increase the digit by 1.

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
 \hline
  \text{hth} & \text{tth} & \text{th} & \text{h} & \text{  t  } & \text{  u  }  \\
  (100,000) & (10,000) & (1,000) & (100) & (10) & (1) \\
 \hline
   6 & 0 & 1 & 4 & 3 & 2  \\
 \hline
 \end{array}
$$

Step 3: Write down the answer with the digits grouped in threes.

$$
591,432+10,000=601,432
$$

heading_path.h1: Chapter 5: Addition and subtraction of integers
heading_path.h2: 5.1 Revise place values

placement.rationale: This exposition revises place value and shows the values of digits in a place-value table.

records.evidence_quote: In Chapter 1 you learnt that the place value of a digit tells us what the value of that digit is, based on its position in a number. You used place value tables to determine the place value of specific digits in a number. For example, the number two million three hundred and five thousand two hundred and fourteen, may
records.content_text:
In Chapter 1 you learnt that the place value of a digit tells us what the value of that digit is, based on its position in a number. You used place value tables to determine the place value of specific digits in a number. For example, the number two million three hundred and five thousand two hundred and fourteen, may be written in a place value table as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
  \hline
    \text{million} &\text{hundred thousand} & \text{ten thousand} & \; \text{thousand} \; & \; \text{hundred} \; & \;\; \text{ten} \;\; & \;\; \text{unit}\;\;  \\
    (1,000,000) & (100,000) & (10,000) & (1,000) & (100) & (10) & (1) \\
    \hline
     2 & 3 & 0 & 5 & 2 & 1 & 4     \\
    \hline
    \end{array}
$$

The place values of the non-zero digits in 2,305,214 are therefore:
$2\times1,000,000=2,000,000$
$3\times100,000=300,000$
$5\times1,000=5,000$
$2\times 100=200$
$1\times10=10$
$4\times1=4$

heading_path.h3: Worked example 5.1: Adding whole numbers

placement.rationale: This worked example adds whole numbers by aligning place values and carrying between columns.

records.evidence_quote: Find the total of $403+628+1,023+49$.
records.prompt_text: Find the total of $403+628+1,023+49$.
records.answer_text:
Step 1: Write the numbers one below the other. Line up the units, tens, hundreds, thousands, and so on.

$$
\begin{array}{r r}
  & \text{th}\, \text{h}\, \text{t}\, \text{u} \\
  & 4\,0\,3 \\
 + & 6\,2\,8 \\
 + & 1,0\,2\,3 \\
 + & 4\,9 \\
 \hline
 \end{array}
$$

Step 2: Add the units column. If the answer is more than 9, write the units of the answer underneath the units column. Write the tens of the answer at the top of the tens column.

$$3+8+3+9=23$$

$$
\begin{array}{r r}
  & \text{th}\, \text{h}\, \text{t}\, \text{u} \\
  &_{2} \,\phantom{0}\\
  & 4\,0\,3 \\
 + & 6\,2\,8 \\
 + & 1,0\,2\,3 \\
 + & 4\,9 \\
 \hline
 &3\\
 \hline
 \end{array}
$$

Step 3: Add the tens column. Include the tens from Step 2. If the answer is more than 9, write the tens of the answer underneath the tens column. Write the hundreds of the answer at the top of the hundreds column.

$$2+0+2+2+4=10$$

$$
\begin{array}{r r}
  & \text{th}\, \text{h}\, \text{t}\, \text{u} \\
  &_{1}\, _{2} \,\phantom{0}\\
  & 4\,0\,3 \\
 + & 6\,2\,8 \\
 + & 1,0\,2\,3 \\
 + & 4\,9 \\
 \hline
 &0\,3\\
 \hline
 \end{array}
$$

Step 4: Repeat Step 3 with the hundreds and thousands. Remember to insert a comma to show thousands.

$$\text{Hundreds}:\space1+4+6+0=11$$
$$\text{Thousands}:\space1+1=2$$

$$
\begin{array}{r r}
  & \text{th}\, \text{h}\, \text{t}\, \text{u} \\
  &_{1}\;\,_1\, _2 \,\phantom{0}\\
  & 4\,0\,3 \\
 + & 6\,2\,8 \\
 + & 1,0\,2\,3 \\
 + & 4\,9 \\
 \hline
 &2,1\,0\,3\\
 \hline
 \end{array}
$$

heading_path.h1: Chapter 5: Addition and subtraction of integers
heading_path.h2: 5.2 Addition and subtraction of large numbers
heading_path.h3: Worked example 5.2: Subtracting whole numbers

placement.rationale: This worked example subtracts whole numbers by aligning place values and regrouping between columns.

records.evidence_quote: Subtract 178 from 4,032.
records.prompt_text: Subtract 178 from 4,032.
records.answer_text:
Step 1: Write the numbers one below the other. Line up the units, tens, hundreds, thousands, and so on.

$$
\begin{array}{r r}
  & \text{th}\, \text{h}\, \text{t}\, \text{u} \\
 & 4,0\,3\,2 \\
         - & 1\,7\,8 \\
 \hline
 \end{array}
$$

Step 2: Subtract the units column. If there are not enough units to subtract from, move one group from the tens column to the units column.

- We cannot subtract 8 from 2.
- There are 3 groups of 10 in the tens column. Move one of them to the units column.
- The units column now has the value $10+2=12$.
- The tens column has only 2 groups of 10 left.

$$
\begin{array}{r r}
  & \text{th}\;\, \text{h}\;\, \text{t}\;\, \text{u}\; \\
  &_{2}\;\,_{12} \\
 & 4,0\,\cancel{3}\cancel{2} \\
         - & 1\;\,7\;8\;\, \\
 \hline
 \end{array}
$$

Now we can subtract the units: $12-8=4$

$$
\begin{array}{r r}
  & \text{th}\;\, \text{h}\;\, \text{t}\;\, \text{u}\; \\
  &_{2}\;\,_{12} \\
 & 4,0\,\cancel{3}\cancel{2} \\
- & 1\;\,7\;8\;\, \\
   \hline
  &4\;\,\\
   \hline
   \end{array}
$$

Step 3: Repeat Step 2 with the tens column. If necessary, move one group from the hundreds column to the tens column.

- We cannot subtract 7 from 2.
- There are no groups in the hundreds column. We must move one group from the thousands column to the hundreds column.
- There are 4 groups of 1,000 in the thousands column. Move one of them to the hundreds column.
- The hundreds column now has 1 group of 1,000. This is equal to 10 groups of 100.
- The thousands column has only 3 groups of 1,000 left.

$$
\begin{array}{r r}
  & \text{th}\phantom{0}\; \text{h}\phantom{0}\; \text{t}\phantom{0} \text{u}\; \\
  &_{3}\;\;_{10}\,\;\;_{2}\,\;_{12}\, \\
 & \cancel{4},\cancel{0}\,\cancel{3}\cancel{2} \\
         - & 1\;\;\,7\;\,8\; \\
 \hline
 &4\;\,\\
 \hline
 \end{array}
$$

Now we can move one group from the hundreds column to the tens column.

The tens column now has 12 groups of 10.
The hundreds column only has 9 groups of 100 left.

$$
\begin{array}{r r}
  & \text{th}\phantom{0}\; \text{h}\phantom{0}\; \text{t}\phantom{0} \text{u}\; \\
  &_{3}\;\;\; _{9}\;\;_{12}\,_{12}\, \\
 & \cancel{4},\cancel{0}\,\cancel{3}\cancel{2} \\
         - & 1\;\;\,7\;\,8\; \\
    \hline
 &4\;\,\\
 \hline
 \end{array}
$$

Now we can subtract the tens: $12-7=5$

$$
\begin{array}{r r}
  & \text{th}\phantom{0}\; \text{h}\phantom{0}\; \text{t}\phantom{0} \text{u}\; \\
  &_{3}\;\;\; _{9}\;\;_{12}\,_{12}\, \\
 & \cancel{4},\cancel{0}\,\cancel{3}\cancel{2} \\
         - & 1\;\;\,7\;\,8\; \\
    \hline
 &5\;\,4\;\\
 \hline
 \end{array}
$$

Step 4: Repeat Step 3 with the hundreds and thousands.

$$\text{Hundreds}:\space9-1=8$$
$$
\begin{array}{r r}
  & \text{th}\phantom{0}\; \text{h}\phantom{0}\; \text{t}\phantom{0} \text{u}\; \\
  &_{3}\;\;\; _{9}\;\;_{12}\,_{12}\, \\
 & \cancel{4},\cancel{0}\,\cancel{3}\cancel{2} \\
         - & 1\;\;\,7\;\,8\; \\
    \hline
 &8\;\;\,5\;\,4\;\\
 \hline
 \end{array}
$$
$$\text{Thousands}:\space3-0=3$$
$$
\begin{array}{r r}
  & \text{th}\phantom{0}\; \text{h}\phantom{0}\; \text{t}\phantom{0} \text{u}\; \\
  &_{3}\;\;\; _{9}\;\;_{12}\,_{12}\, \\

records.content_text:
- The place value of a digit tells us what the value of that digit is, based on its position in a number.
- When we add or subtract large numbers, we line up the units, tens, hundreds and thousands of the numbers.
- A number line is a straight line, divided into equal segments, that shows the positions of numbers.
- Positive numbers are larger than zero and lie to the right of zero on a number line.
- Negative numbers are smaller than zero and lie to the left of zero on a number line.
- Zero is neither positive nor negative.
- The symbol < means "smaller than", and 3<5 means three is smaller than five. The symbol > means "greater than", and 5>3 means five is greater than three.
- When we add one integer to another, we may see it as units that are added along the number line. When we add positive numbers, we count to the right on a number line. When we add negative numbers, we count to the left on a number line.
- Subtracting a number is the same as adding the "opposite" of the number. For example, $2-7$ is the same as $2+(-7)$.
- Subtraction may also be seen as the difference between two numbers. For example, there are 5 units between the numbers 2 and 7. If the number which is subtracted from lies to the negative side of the number that is subtracted, the difference is negative: $2-7=-5$. If the number which is subtracted from lies to the positive side of the number that is subtracted, the difference is positive: $7-2=5$.
- A thermometer is an instrument used to measure temperature. Temperatures above $0\space ^\circ\text C$ are positive. Temperatures below $0\space ^\circ\text C$ are negative.
- A positive bank balance means you have money in the bank. A negative bank balance means you owe the bank money.
- For movement along a straight line, we take one direction as positive. The opposite direction is negative.
